Latin.note: The appeal to Jonathan survives. The Greek comparison with the return from Babylon has no identifiable separate counterpart in this Latin interval.
The Latin fear clause continues into the following interval, XIII.38, where Jonathan and the ensuing policy identify the new Greek section. The original sentence and order are preserved.

This interval begins within the Latin fear clause carried from XIII.37. The reference to Jonathan and the policy of gathering forces and returning hostages correspond to Greek XIII.38; no sentence has been rewritten.
The Latin travel account compresses the many-temples material corresponding to the opening of Greek XIII.66. The independent XIII.66 interval starts with the irregular temples and discord.

The many-temples claim at the Greek opening is compressed into the preceding Latin travel account, XIII.65. This selection starts with the irregular temples and discord; the transmitted syntax is preserved.
The task of persuading the hostile Antiochenes survives here. The success described at the end of Greek XIII.111 is expressed later in the transmitted Latin explanation within XIII.115.
This interval includes the success of the Antiochene settlement corresponding to the ending of Greek XIII.111. The intervening Latin explanation and transmitted order are preserved.
The closing phrase “ad arabiam eum fugauit” corresponds to the opening flight to Arabia in Greek XIII.117. XIII.117's independent Latin interval starts with Ptolemy's fall from his horse.
The flight to Arabia at the Greek opening survives earlier at the end of XIII.116: “ad arabiam eum fugauit”. This interval starts with Ptolemy's fall from his horse, wounds and incapacity.
The garrison's request survives in compressed wording. Its explicit Greek destination, Demetrius, is not separately named in this Latin interval.

Senatorial confirmation is expressed as a relative clause recalling prior enactments, followed by safe-conduct letters. The Greek reference to Europe is not independently named here. The changed Latin syntax and tense are preserved.
The Parthian campaign and eventual capture survive; the Greek account of defeat in battle is compressed in the Latin. The transmitted sequence is preserved.
The Latin describes death where the corresponding Greek account concerns capture. This transmitted wording is retained without correction from the Greek.

The appended documentary dating formula, “in mutuis documentis publicisque monumentis primi anni simonis benefactoris et iudaeorum principis scriptum est.”, survives here in latin-book13-num208 and corresponds to Greek XIII.214. Its continuation, the prosperity-and-victories statement, is displayed in the Latin interval for XIII.214. This partial correspondence is distributed between two physical intervals; the transmitted wording and sequence are preserved, and the cause of the altered correspondence is unknown.

No independent Latin interval. The full reviewed Latin context has no identifiable counterpart of this section's separate account of Simon's appointment as high priest, liberation from Macedonian tribute and the 170-year chronology. The documentary dating formula within XIII.212 corresponds to Greek XIII.214 and does not supply this liberation account. The earlier military appointment in latin-book13-num201 is a different account. Greek and English remain independently accessible; no cause, physical loss or tradition-wide absence is inferred.

Partial correspondence distributed between two physical intervals. The documentary dating formula corresponding to Greek XIII.214 survives earlier within the Latin interval for XIII.212, in latin-book13-num208, at “in mutuis documentis publicisque monumentis primi anni simonis benefactoris et iudaeorum principis scriptum est.” This interval begins with the ensuing prosperity-and-victories statement, “Itaque iudaei feliciter aduersarios uicinos superauerunt,”. The earlier dating material is not absent. The wording and existing sequence are preserved; the cause of the altered correspondence is unknown.

No independent Latin interval. The full reviewed Latin context has no identifiable counterpart of this section's assembly persuasion and warnings about the former garrison and possible foreign restoration. The neighbouring collective demolition survives in XIII.217; it is not reassigned to manufacture an interval here. Greek and English remain independently accessible; no cause, physical loss or tradition-wide absence is inferred.

Collective demolition, continuous work and the temple's prominence survive here. The Greek concluding formula about Simon's deeds resumes within the following Latin interval, XIII.218. The full assembly persuasion is not independently represented in the reviewed adjoining transcription.

This interval includes “ea quae temporibus symonis gesta sunt hunc contirient modum”, corresponding to the ending of Greek XIII.217, between repeated “Post captiuitatem” openings. The simulated surgical death in Greek XIII.218 is not separately represented. All repetitions and transmitted order are preserved.
The siege and water shortage survive. The relieving rain and setting of the Pleiades in the Greek ending have no identifiable separate counterparts in the reviewed Latin context.

Only the closing contempt of both brothers survives here: “ambosque inter se dimicantes contemnens”. The opening ravaging by Cyzicenus and loss of Egyptian allies have no separately identifiable counterparts in this transcription. The surviving tail remains in its transmitted syntax.
The capture and destruction of Samaria survive; the Greek account of flooding is not separately expressed in this interval.
The request for correction and ensuing praise survive. The Greek opening assertion about Pharisaic philosophy has no separately identifiable counterpart here.
The accusation of royal pretensions and intended murder survives. The Greek final rationale about shared royal honour has no separate counterpart in the reviewed Latin interval.
Salome's release of the brothers and Alexander's appointment survive. The concluding Greek account of moderation is not separately expressed here.
The closing Latin wording compresses the Zoilus and Gaza appeal corresponding to the opening of Greek XIII.334. XIII.334's independent interval begins with Alexander raising the siege.
The initial Zoilus and Gaza appeal is compressed into changed wording at the end of XIII.333. This selection starts with Alexander raising the siege and feigning friendship; no text has been moved.
The capture of Ptolemais survives. The Greek corroborating statement about Strabo and Nicolaus has no independently identifiable Latin counterpart in this interval.
Grypus's murder survives, with the transmitted age retained. The Greek twenty-nine-year reign is not separately stated here.
The inducements, victory and hired soldiers' deaths survive. The Greek appraisal of loyal courage and Demetrius's own casualties have no separate counterparts in the reviewed Latin ending.

The transfer to Antioch and Syrian rule has a damaged connection in this transcription: Philip is not distinctly named, and “statim ad antiochiam perrexit” repeats. The wording and repetition are preserved without reconstruction.
The request for assignment to fortresses survives. The Greek concluding account of humble personal existence is not separately represented here.
The unnamed queen's resistance and Jewish appeal survive. The Greek identification as Selene/Cleopatra is not independently supplied in this Latin interval.
Support, fortress captures and recruitment survive. The Greek concluding explanation of allies' wealth and expected rewards has no separately identifiable counterpart here.

The assessment of misery after death and peace during the queen's rule survives, including the repeated “mortem compleuit”. The announcement of the next book printed in Niese has no separate Latin counterpart here; Loeb places that announcement in its apparatus. The transmitted ending is preserved without reconstruction.
